newsitem.title: UK: Mark steady in Europe, awaits German tax estimates.
newsitem.headline: Mark steady in Europe, awaits German tax estimates.

text.p: The mark was mixed on its European crosses in morning trade, largely ignoring a slump in the dollar and mark against the yen which also pressured dollar/mark.
Optimism of a broad-based, timely start to Europe's monetary union continued to support the peripherals though dealers said activity was thin, overshadowed by the dollar/yen slump.

The focus was on the official estimates of Germany's 1997 tax revenues due today. German coalition sources have indicated the revenues will fall nearly 20 billion marks short of previous forecasts, cutting Germany's chances of meeting the EMU budget deficit criteria unless bold action is taken to trim spending.

"Expectations are for an overshoot of 15-20 billion marks. This will lift the deficit to 3.1 percent, or some 3.3 percent if you include higher unemployment," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago.

While this puts Germany above the EMU 3.0 percent deficit/GDP threshold, market sentiment has opted for a broad-based EMU start with a flexible interpretation of the deficit criteria which has provided support for the mark's satellites.

However, Knuthsen said the risk was for Germany's tax revenue shortfall to come in much larger than expectations -- a major blow to the EMU project which would be seen as positive for the mark at the expense of its European neighbours.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said today he would oppose any softening of the EMU criteria. On Wednesday he indicated he planned a series of measures to plug the tax revenue hole and expressed confidence Germany would be in EMU.
German press reports said today Waigel was seeking a higher value of Bundesbank assets to boost the central bank's profits in a bid to raise further cash for the government's budget.

The German finance ministry, responding to a German press report today, said it had no plans to sell gold to aid the budget and a Eurostat official said the rule that gold sales cannot be used to cut deficits applied across the EU.
However, coalition sources confirmed that plans have been drawn up in this direction and news that Waigel would attend today's Bundesbank council meeting set market tongues wagging.
Meantime, German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said Germany was against any EMU delay.
Mark/lira firmed slightly from early lows but the lira still looked well-supported, mainly on EMU optimism and the prospect of a near-term cut in Italian interest rates.

This week's low inflation data for Spain and Portugal have reinforced this view, but analysts said the Bank of Italy may choose to wait for the presentation of the government's three-year economic plan due at the end of this month before deciding on a rate move.
Mark/lira was trading at 985.85/15 at 0914 GMT versus 984.75/5.25 in late Europe on Wednesday.

The mark was little changed against the French franc from Wednesday, holding at 3.3679/84 against 3.3677/80. The latest French opinion polls continue to show the ruling centre-right in the lead ahead of the May 25/June 1 parliamentary election.

Mark/peseta was easier with Wednesday's low inflation data reinforcing expectations of a Spanish repo rate cut as soon as Friday. Activity was muted, however, by today's holiday in Spain. Mark/peseta was at 84.36/38 versus 84.41/42 Wednesday.
